title: Continuity
summary: A function is continuous at a point when the limit equals the value. On a closed interval that forces the intermediate-value and extreme-value theorems.
intuition:
Continuity is the sentence $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$. The limit has to exist, $f(a)$ has to be defined, and those two numbers have to be the same. A hole, a wrong value, a jump, or a vertical asymptote each breaks a different part of that sentence.

The intermediate value theorem turns continuity on a closed interval into a guarantee about hitting heights. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $k$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, some point of $(a,b)$ is sent to $k$. The theorem does not say the point is unique. A jump can skip a height entirely, which is why the continuity hypothesis is doing the work.

On a closed bounded interval, continuity is even stronger. The extreme value theorem says $f$ is bounded and attains both a maximum and a minimum. The open interval $(0,1)$ with $f(x)=x$ shows why the endpoints matter: the values get arbitrarily close to $1$ and never reach it. Finding those attained extrema is the optimization lesson; this lesson only records that they exist.

Discontinuities that the syllabus asks you to name are removable, jump, and infinite. A removable discontinuity has a finite limit that is not the function value, or the function is missing at that point. A jump has finite one-sided limits that disagree. An infinite discontinuity has a vertical blow-up, so the limit is not a real number.

definitions.body: $f$ is continuous at $a$ when $f(a)$ is defined, $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists as a real number, and the two are equal. Continuity on an interval means continuity at every point of that interval, with one-sided limits at an included endpoint.
The limit $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists and is finite, but $f(a)$ is undefined or $f(a)$ is not that limit. Defining or redefining $f(a)$ to be the limit removes the discontinuity.
Both one-sided limits exist and are finite, and they are not equal. The jump size is the absolute difference of those two limits. No single value of $f(a)$ can match both sides.

At least one one-sided limit is $+\infty$ or $-\infty$, as with $1/x$ at $0$. The limit is not a real number, so the continuity equality cannot hold. This is not a jump, because a jump requires finite one-sided limits.

Intermediate value theorem: a function continuous on $[a,b]$ attains every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. Extreme value theorem: a function continuous on $[a,b]$ is bounded and attains its maximum and its minimum somewhere in $[a,b]$.

formulas.name: Continuity criterion
formulas.note: All three ingredients are required: $f(a)$ defined, the limit existing, and equality.

formulas.name: Intermediate value theorem
formulas.note: Hypothesis: $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a,b]$. The point $c$ need not be unique. The same statement holds if $f(b)<k<f(a)$.

formulas.name: Extreme value theorem
formulas.note: Hypothesis: $f$ is continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$. The theorem says the max and min are attained. It does not locate them.

formulas.name: Removable repair
formulas.note: This produces a function continuous at $a$. It is available only when the two-sided limit exists and is finite.

properties: Polynomials, $e^{x}$, $\sin$, and $\cos$ are continuous at every real point. $\ln$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$. A rational function is continuous at every point where the denominator is not zero.
A sum, product, and quotient of continuous functions is continuous where the expression is defined. A composition of continuous functions is continuous on the set where the composition is defined.
The intermediate value theorem implies that a continuous function on $[a,b]$ with $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ of opposite signs has a root in $(a,b)$. It does not count the roots.
Continuity on a closed interval implies boundedness and attainment of both a maximum and a minimum. Continuity on an open interval does not: $f(x)=1/x$ on $(0,1)$ is continuous and unbounded.
Equal one-sided limits are not enough for continuity unless they also equal $f(a)$. That gap is exactly a removable discontinuity when the common limit is finite.

examples.title: A removable hole with the wrong value
examples.prompt: Define $f(x)=(x^{2}-9)/(x-3)$ for $x\neq 3$ and $f(3)=9$. Classify the discontinuity at $3$, and repair it.
steps: For $x\neq 3$, factor $x^{2}-9=(x-3)(x+3)$ and cancel the common factor, getting $f(x)=x+3$. Cancellation is legal only away from $3$.
The two-sided limit is $\lim_{x\to 3}(x+3)=6$. Both one-sided limits equal $6$, so the discontinuity is not a jump and not infinite.
The function value is $f(3)=9$, and $9\neq 6$. The limit exists, but it does not equal the value, so $f$ is not continuous at $3$.
Defining $f(3)=6$ makes the value match the limit. The repaired function is $x+3$ at every point, which is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.
examples.answer: The discontinuity at $3$ is removable. The continuous repair is $f(3)=6$, not the given value $9$.

examples.title: A jump that skips a value, and an attained maximum
examples.prompt: Let $g(x)=-1$ for $x<0$ and $g(x)=1$ for $x\geq 0$. Let $p(x)=x^{2}$ on $[-2,3]$. Show that $g$ skips the value $0$, and find the max and min of $p$.
steps: The left-hand limit of $g$ at $0$ is $-1$ and the right-hand limit is $1$. Both are finite and they differ, so $g$ has a jump discontinuity at $0$. No choice of $g(0)$ matches both sides.

On $[-1,1]$, every value of $g$ is either $-1$ or $1$. The number $0$ lies between $g(-1)=-1$ and $g(1)=1$, but it is never attained. The intermediate value theorem does not apply, because $g$ is not continuous on $[-1,1]$.
$p(x)=x^{2}$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous on the closed interval $[-2,3]$. The extreme value theorem says the maximum and the minimum are attained.
The critical point of $p$ inside $(-2,3)$ is where $p'(x)=2x=0$, so $x=0$, and $p(0)=0$. The endpoint values are $p(-2)=4$ and $p(3)=9$. The attained minimum is $0$ and the attained maximum is $9$.
examples.answer: $g$ jumps at $0$ and never takes the value $0$. On $[-2,3]$, $p$ attains minimum $0$ at $x=0$ and maximum $9$ at $x=3$.

traps: Calling $f$ continuous because the two-sided limit exists. Continuity also demands that the limit equal $f(a)$. A wrong filled-in value is still a discontinuity, and it is removable.
Using the intermediate value theorem on a jump. Opposite signs of $g(-1)$ and $g(1)$ do not produce a root when $g$ skips every height strictly between $-1$ and $1$.
Expecting a maximum on an open interval. The identity function on $(0,1)$ is continuous, and it has no maximum in the interval.
Labelling $1/x$ at $0$ a jump. The one-sided limits are infinite, so the discontinuity is infinite. A jump requires both one-sided limits to be finite.

questions.stem: Define $f(x)=(x^{2}-9)/(x-3)$ for $x\neq 3$ and set $f(3)=9$. The discontinuity of $f$ at $x=3$ is
options: not a discontinuity, because $f(3)$ is defined
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, removable.

For $x\neq 3$, $f(x)=x+3$, so both one-sided limits equal $6$. The limit exists and is finite, which rules out a jump and an infinite discontinuity. The stored value $f(3)=9$ is not $6$, so $f$ is discontinuous, and resetting $f(3)$ to $6$ removes the break. Defining a value does not create continuity unless the value equals the limit.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=x^{3}+x-1$ on the closed interval $[0,1]$. Which statement is true?
options: There is at least one $c$ in $(0,1)$ with $f(c)=0$.
$f$ has no root in $(0,1)$ because $f(0)$ and $f(1)$ are both nonzero.
The intermediate value theorem still applies on $[0,1]$ if $f$ is redefined to jump at $1/2$.
$f(1/2)<0$ proves that $f$ has no root in $(0,1)$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

$f$ is a polynomial, so it is continuous on $[0,1]$. The endpoint values are $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=1+1-1=1$. Since $0$ lies between $-1$ and $1$, the intermediate value theorem supplies a root in $(0,1)$.

Nonzero endpoint values are the reason the theorem applies, not a reason there is no root. A jump at $1/2$ would remove the continuity hypothesis. And $f(1/2)=(1/8)+(1/2)-1=-3/8<0$, while $f(1)=1$, so the sign change on $[1/2,1]$ still produces a root.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: A function continuous on a closed bounded interval is bounded and attains its maximum and its minimum.
A function continuous on an open interval always attains its maximum.
A jump discontinuity has finite, unequal one-sided limits.
If $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A and C**.

A is the extreme value theorem. C is the definition of a jump used in this lesson: both one-sided limits exist, both are finite, and they differ.

B fails for $f(x)=x$ on $(0,1)$, which has no maximum. D confuses continuity with differentiability. The equality $\lim f=f(a)$ is continuity. The absolute-value function satisfies it at $0$ and is not differentiable there.

questions.stem: Define $f(x)=x+1$ for $x<2$, $f(2)=5$, and $f(x)=x+2$ for $x>2$. Which of the following are true?
options: The left-hand limit of $f$ at $2$ is $3$.
$f$ is continuous at every point of the interval $[0,1]$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, C, and D**.

From the left, $f(x)=x+1\to 3$. From the right, $f(x)=x+2\to 4$. The one-sided limits are finite and unequal, so the discontinuity is a jump. The stored value $5$ matches neither side.

Setting $f(2)=3$ matches the left-hand limit only. The right-hand limit is still $4$, so the two-sided limit still does not exist and the discontinuity remains. On $[0,1]$ the formula is the polynomial $x+1$, whose only candidate problem in the definition sits at $2$, outside this interval.

questions.stem: For $x\neq 2$, let $f(x)=(x^{2}-4)/(x-2)$. Enter the integer $k$ such that defining $f(2)=k$ makes $f$ continuous at $2$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **4**.

Factor $x^{2}-4=(x-2)(x+2)$. For $x\neq 2$ the quotient simplifies to $x+2$. Therefore $\lim_{x\to 2}f(x)=2+2=4$. Continuity requires $f(2)$ to equal that limit, so $k=4$.
